flashcards.question: What is economics, and what are its two key elements?
flashcards.answer:
Economics is the study of how societies use scarce resources to produce valuable goods and services and distribute them among different people.
The two key elements are:
• Scarcity — resources are limited
• Efficiency — using those resources to get the most value

flashcards.question: What are the three problems of economic organization?
flashcards.answer:
1. WHAT goods are produced (and in what quantities)
2. HOW goods are produced (with which resources/technology)
3. FOR WHOM goods are produced (who gets them)

flashcards.question: Positive vs. normative economics — what is the difference?
flashcards.answer:
Positive economics describes the FACTS of the economy ("a higher minimum wage raises unemployment among the young").
Normative economics involves VALUE JUDGMENTS — what ought to be ("taxes should be progressive").

flashcards.question: How do microeconomics and macroeconomics differ?
flashcards.answer:
Microeconomics studies the behavior of individual economic units — consumers, firms, workers, investors — and how prices allocate scarce resources.
Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole (growth, inflation, unemployment, business cycles).
flashcards.explanation: Adam Smith → micro (the "invisible hand"); Keynes → macro.

flashcards.question: What are inputs, outputs, and the factors of production?
flashcards.answer:
Inputs are commodities/services used to produce things; outputs are the goods/services that result.
The three factors of production are:
• Land (natural resources)
• Labor
• Capital

flashcards.question: What is the production-possibility frontier (PPF)?
flashcards.answer:
The PPF shows the maximum quantity of goods an economy can efficiently produce given its technology and available inputs.
• On the frontier → efficient
• Inside → inefficient (idle resources)
• Outside → currently unattainable

flashcards.question: How does the PPF illustrate opportunity cost?
flashcards.answer: Along the frontier, producing more of one good means giving up some of the other. The opportunity cost is the amount of the OTHER good sacrificed — shown by the (magnitude of the) slope of the PPF.
flashcards.explanation: The PPF bows outward → rising opportunity cost.

flashcards.question: What causes the PPF to shift outward?
flashcards.answer: Economic growth: more inputs (labor, capital, resources) or better technology. Investing in capital goods today (sacrificing current consumption) shifts the future PPF outward.

flashcards.question: What is productive efficiency?
flashcards.answer: An economy is productively efficient when it cannot produce more of one good without producing less of another — i.e. it operates ON its production-possibility frontier.

flashcards.question: Real vs. nominal prices — what is the difference?
flashcards.answer:
The nominal price is a good’s absolute price in current dollars. The real price is the price relative to an aggregate measure of prices (corrected for inflation), so values from different years can be compared:
\( \text{Real price} = \text{Nominal price}\times\dfrac{\text{CPI}_{\text{base}}}{\text{CPI}_{\text{current}}} \)

flashcards.question: What is a market, and what is arbitrage?
flashcards.answer:
A market is a collection of buyers and sellers that, through their interaction, determine the price of a good. The EXTENT of a market is its boundaries (geographic and by product range).
Arbitrage is buying at a low price in one place and selling at a higher price in another.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between a theory and a model in economics?
flashcards.answer: A theory explains observed phenomena using a set of basic rules and assumptions. A model is a mathematical representation (of a firm, market, etc.) based on that theory. No theory is perfectly correct — it is judged by its predictions.

learn.content:
Preliminaries — the economic way of thinking

Economics studies how societies use scarce resources to produce valuable goods and services and distribute them among people. Its two pillars are scarcity (resources are limited) and efficiency (getting the most from them). Every economy must answer three questions: what to produce, how, and for whom.

Positive vs. normative

Positive economics describes what is (testable facts). Normative economics expresses what ought to be (value judgments). "A carbon tax cuts emissions" is positive; "we should tax carbon" is normative.

Production-possibility frontier (PPF)

The PPF shows the maximum output of two goods an economy can produce with its given technology and inputs (land, labor, capital).

  • On the frontier → productively efficient
  • Inside → inefficient (idle resources)
  • Outside → currently unattainable

Because resources are not equally good at everything, the frontier bows outward, so the opportunity cost — the other good given up — rises as you specialize. Growth (more inputs or better technology) shifts the whole PPF outward.

Markets and prices

A market is the buyers and sellers whose interaction sets a good’s price. Arbitrage (buy low here, sell high there) tends to equalize prices within a market. To compare prices across years we adjust for inflation:

\[ \text{Real price} = \text{Nominal price}\times\frac{\text{CPI}_{\text{base}}}{\text{CPI}_{\text{current}}} \]

Microeconomics is about individual units (consumers, firms, workers) and how prices allocate scarce resources — much of it is about limits, and making the most of them.

flashcards.question: What is a demand schedule, and why does the demand curve slope downward?
flashcards.answer:
A demand schedule is the relationship between a good’s market price and the quantity buyers demand, holding other things constant; its graph is the demand curve.
It slopes downward (the law of downward-sloping demand) for two reasons:
• the substitution effect
• the income effect
flashcards.explanation: Market demand is found by adding the quantities demanded by all individuals at each price.

flashcards.question: Movement ALONG the demand curve vs. a SHIFT of the demand curve — what triggers each?
flashcards.answer:
A change in the good’s OWN price → a movement along the curve (a change in quantity demanded).
A change in ANY OTHER factor (income, prices of related goods, tastes…) → a shift of the whole curve (a change in demand).
flashcards.explanation: Mixing up the two is the most common exam mistake.

flashcards.question: Which factors SHIFT the demand curve (besides the good’s own price)?
flashcards.answer:
• Average income
• Size of the market (number of buyers)
• Prices & availability of related goods (substitutes / complements)
• Tastes and preferences
• Special / expectational influences

flashcards.question: Which forces SHIFT the supply curve (besides the good’s own price)?
flashcards.answer:
• Cost of production
• Prices of inputs (labor, energy, machinery)
• Technology (lowers inputs needed per unit)
• Prices of related (substitute) outputs
• Government policy (taxes, regulation)
• Special influences (e.g. weather)

flashcards.question: What is market equilibrium?
flashcards.answer: The price and quantity at which the forces of supply and demand are in balance. At the equilibrium (market-clearing) price, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: \(Q_d = Q_s\).
flashcards.explanation: Above equilibrium → surplus (excess supply); below it → shortage (excess demand).

flashcards.question: If DEMAND rises (curve shifts right), what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
flashcards.answer: Both rise: equilibrium price ↑ and equilibrium quantity ↑.
flashcards.explanation: Demand falls → both ↓. Supply rises → price ↓, quantity ↑. Supply falls → price ↑, quantity ↓.

flashcards.question: Define the price elasticity of demand and give its formula.
flashcards.answer:
The percentage change in quantity demanded resulting from a 1% change in price:
\(E_p = \dfrac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P} = \dfrac{P}{Q}\cdot\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta P}\).
It is normally negative; we usually report its absolute value.

flashcards.question: How do you classify demand as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic from \(E_p\)?
flashcards.answer:
• \(|E_p| > 1\) → elastic (quantity very responsive)
• \(|E_p| < 1\) → inelastic (quantity barely responds)
• \(|E_p| = 1\) → unit elastic

flashcards.question: What is the arc (midpoint) elasticity formula, and why use it?
flashcards.answer:
\(E_p = \dfrac{\Delta Q \,/\, \tfrac{Q_1+Q_2}{2}}{\Delta P \,/\, \tfrac{P_1+P_2}{2}}\).
It uses the AVERAGE of the two prices and quantities as the base, so you get the same elasticity whether price rises or falls between the two points.

flashcards.question: Is the slope of a demand curve the same as its elasticity?
flashcards.answer: No. Slope \(=\Delta P/\Delta Q\) is constant on a straight line, but elasticity \(=\dfrac{P}{Q}\cdot\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta P}\) varies along it: demand is elastic near the top (high \(P\), low \(Q\)) and inelastic near the bottom.

flashcards.question: Define income elasticity of demand.
flashcards.answer:
The percentage change in quantity demanded resulting from a 1% increase in income:
\(E_I = \dfrac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta I}\).
\(E_I > 0\) → normal good; \(E_I < 0\) → inferior good.

flashcards.question: Define cross-price elasticity of demand.
flashcards.answer:
The percentage change in quantity demanded of good A from a 1% increase in the price of good B:
\(E_{Q_A P_B} = \dfrac{\%\Delta Q_A}{\%\Delta P_B}\).
Positive → substitutes; negative → complements.

flashcards.question: How does price elasticity relate to total revenue?
flashcards.answer: Revenue is \(R = P \times Q\). If demand is elastic (\(|E_p|>1\)), a price cut RAISES revenue; if inelastic (\(|E_p|<1\)), a price cut LOWERS revenue; if unit elastic, revenue is unchanged.

flashcards.question: What are completely inelastic and infinitely elastic demand?
flashcards.answer:
Completely (perfectly) inelastic: \(E_p = 0\) → a vertical demand curve (quantity fixed regardless of price).
Infinitely (perfectly) elastic: \(E_p = \infty\) → a horizontal demand curve (any quantity at a single price).

learn.content:
The Basics of Supply & Demand

Demand describes how much of a good buyers will purchase at each price, other things equal. The law of downward-sloping demand says quantity demanded rises as price falls, driven by the substitution effect and the income effect. Supply describes how much producers are willing to sell at each price. Either schedule can shift when something other than the good’s own price changes.

Movement vs. shift — the #1 exam trap

A change in the good’s own price → a movement along the curve. A change in any other factor (income, prices of related goods, tastes, technology, taxes…) → a shift of the whole curve.

Market equilibrium

Equilibrium is the price and quantity where supply and demand balance — the market-clearing price, where

\[ Q_d = Q_s \]

Above the equilibrium price there is a surplus (excess supply); below it, a shortage (excess demand). If demand rises, both equilibrium price and quantity rise; if supply rises, price falls but quantity rises.

Price elasticity of demand

Elasticity is the percentage change in one variable caused by a 1% change in another. The price elasticity of demand is

\[ E_p = \frac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P} = \frac{\Delta Q / Q}{\Delta P / P} = \frac{P}{Q}\cdot\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta P} \]

It is normally negative (price up, quantity down); we usually quote its absolute value \(|E_p|\):

  • \(|E_p| > 1\) → elastic (quantity very responsive)
  • \(|E_p| < 1\) → inelastic
  • \(|E_p| = 1\) → unit elastic

To get the same answer whether price rises or falls between two points, use the arc (midpoint) formula, which takes the averages as the base:

\[ E_p = \frac{\Delta Q \,/\, \tfrac{Q_1 + Q_2}{2}}{\Delta P \,/\, \tfrac{P_1 + P_2}{2}} \]

Worked example — midpoint method

Price rises from \(P_1 = 90\) to \(P_2 = 110\); quantity falls from \(Q_1 = 240\) to \(Q_2 = 160\).

Step 1 — changes: \(\Delta P = 110 - 90 = 20\), \(\Delta Q = 160 - 240 = -80\).

Step 2 — percentages off the midpoints (\(\bar P = 100\), \(\bar Q = 200\)):

\[ \%\Delta P = \frac{20}{100} = 20\%, \qquad \%\Delta Q = \frac{-80}{200} = -40\% \]

Step 3 — divide:

\[ E_p = \frac{-40\%}{20\%} = -2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad |E_p| = 2 \]

Demand here is elastic: a 1% price rise cuts quantity by about 2%.

Income and cross-price elasticities

Income elasticity measures responsiveness to income:

\[ E_I = \frac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta I} \]

\(E_I > 0\) → normal good; \(E_I < 0\) → inferior good. Cross-price elasticity measures the response of good A to the price of good B:

\[ E_{Q_A P_B} = \frac{\%\Delta Q_A}{\%\Delta P_B} \]

Positive → substitutes; negative → complements.

Elasticity and revenue

Since revenue \(R = P \times Q\): if demand is elastic, a price cut raises revenue; if inelastic, a price cut lowers revenue; if unit elastic, revenue is unchanged.

Remember: slope ≠ elasticity. Along a straight-line demand curve the slope is constant, but demand is elastic near the top (high price, low quantity) and inelastic near the bottom.

flashcards.question: What three steps make up the theory of consumer behavior?
flashcards.answer:
1. Consumer preferences — what the consumer likes (indifference curves)
2. Budget constraints — what the consumer can afford
3. Consumer choices — combining the two to maximize satisfaction

flashcards.question: What three basic assumptions do we make about preferences?
flashcards.answer:
• Completeness — the consumer can rank any two baskets
• Transitivity — if A ⪰ B and B ⪰ C, then A ⪰ C
• More is better than less (goods are desirable)

flashcards.question: What is an indifference curve?
flashcards.answer: A curve showing all combinations of market baskets that give the consumer the SAME level of satisfaction. A whole set of them is an indifference map; higher curves = more satisfaction.
flashcards.explanation: Indifference curves can never intersect (it would violate transitivity).

flashcards.question: What is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS)?
flashcards.answer:
The maximum amount of one good a consumer will give up to get one more unit of another, holding satisfaction constant. It equals the magnitude of the slope of the indifference curve:
\( MRS = -\dfrac{\Delta C}{\Delta F} = \dfrac{MU_F}{MU_C} \)

flashcards.question: Why are indifference curves typically convex (bowed inward)?
flashcards.answer: Because of a DIMINISHING marginal rate of substitution: the more of good F you already have, the less of good C you are willing to give up for another unit of F.

flashcards.question: What is utility, and what is the difference between ordinal and cardinal utility?
flashcards.answer:
Utility is a numerical score for the satisfaction from a basket; a utility function assigns it.
• Ordinal utility only RANKS baskets (most→least preferred)
• Cardinal utility says by HOW MUCH one basket is preferred to another

flashcards.question: Write the budget line and state its slope.
flashcards.answer:
With income \(I\) and prices \(P_F, P_C\):
\( P_F F + P_C C = I \).
Its slope is \(-\dfrac{P_F}{P_C}\) — the rate at which the market lets you trade C for F.

flashcards.question: How does the budget line move when (a) income changes, (b) one price changes?
flashcards.answer:
(a) A change in income (prices fixed) shifts the budget line PARALLEL — outward if income rises, inward if it falls.
(b) A change in one good’s price PIVOTS the line, changing its slope (the intercept on that good’s axis moves).

flashcards.question: What two conditions define the consumer’s optimal (utility-maximizing) basket?
flashcards.answer:
1. It lies ON the budget line (all income spent)
2. It is on the highest attainable indifference curve
This happens where the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line:
\( MRS = \dfrac{P_F}{P_C} \)

flashcards.question: What is marginal utility, and what is diminishing marginal utility?
flashcards.answer: Marginal utility (MU) is the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good. Diminishing marginal utility: as you consume more of a good, each additional unit adds less utility.

flashcards.question: State the equal-marginal principle.
flashcards.answer:
Utility is maximized when the marginal utility per dollar is equal across all goods:
\( \dfrac{MU_F}{P_F} = \dfrac{MU_C}{P_C} \).
This is equivalent to \(MRS = P_F/P_C\).

flashcards.question: What is a corner solution?
flashcards.answer: An optimum where the consumer buys NONE of one good (the best basket is at an end of the budget line). There the tangency condition need not hold — \(MRS \ne P_F/P_C\).

learn.content:
Consumer Behavior

Consumer theory explains how people split limited income among goods to maximize satisfaction. It has three building blocks: preferences, budget constraints, and the resulting choice.

Preferences and indifference curves

We assume preferences are complete (any two baskets can be ranked), transitive, and that more is better. An indifference curve joins all baskets giving equal satisfaction; higher curves are preferred, and curves never cross. Their slope is the marginal rate of substitution:

\[ MRS = -\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta F} = \frac{MU_F}{MU_C} \]

Curves are convex because the MRS diminishes: the more F you have, the less C you will trade for one more F.

The budget constraint

With income \(I\) and prices \(P_F\) and \(P_C\), affordable baskets satisfy the budget line:

\[ P_F F + P_C C = I, \qquad \text{slope} = -\frac{P_F}{P_C} \]

A change in income shifts the line in parallel; a change in one price pivots it.

The consumer’s optimum

Satisfaction is highest where the budget line is tangent to an indifference curve — the marginal benefit of a good (its MRS) equals its marginal cost (the price ratio):

\[ MRS = \frac{P_F}{P_C} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{MU_F}{P_F} = \frac{MU_C}{P_C} \]

This is the equal-marginal principle: at the optimum the marginal utility per dollar is the same for every good.

If \(MRS \ne P_F/P_C\), the consumer can do better by reallocating spending — unless the optimum is a corner solution (zero of one good).

flashcards.question: How is an individual demand curve derived from consumer theory?
flashcards.answer: By tracing the optimal quantity of a good as its price changes (the price-consumption path). At every point on the demand curve the consumer is maximizing utility, but the level of utility changes as you move along it.

flashcards.question: What is an Engel curve?
flashcards.answer: A curve relating the quantity of a good consumed to the consumer’s INCOME (holding prices fixed). It slopes upward for normal goods and downward (eventually) for inferior goods.

flashcards.question: Normal vs. inferior goods — define each.
flashcards.answer:
• Normal good: quantity demanded RISES when income rises (positive income elasticity).
• Inferior good: quantity demanded FALLS when income rises (negative income elasticity).

flashcards.question: Decompose the effect of a price fall into its two parts.
flashcards.answer:
Total effect = substitution effect + income effect.
• Substitution effect: the good is now relatively cheaper → buy more of it (always opposite to the price change).
• Income effect: real purchasing power rises → buy more (normal good) or less (inferior good).

flashcards.question: Why can the income effect work "backwards" for an inferior good?
flashcards.answer: For an inferior good, a rise in real income (from a price fall) reduces quantity demanded. The income effect then opposes the substitution effect. If it ever outweighs it, you get a Giffen good (upward-sloping demand) — very rare.

flashcards.question: How is the market demand curve obtained from individual demands?
flashcards.answer: By adding the quantities demanded by all individuals at each price — i.e. the HORIZONTAL sum of the individual demand curves. The market curve is flatter (more elastic) and reflects more buyers.

flashcards.question: What is consumer surplus?
flashcards.answer: The difference between the maximum a consumer is willing to pay and what they actually pay. Graphically it is the area BELOW the demand curve and ABOVE the market price.

flashcards.question: What are network externalities (bandwagon vs. snob effect)?
flashcards.answer:
A network externality occurs when one person’s demand depends on others’ purchases.
• Bandwagon effect (positive): you want it because others have it → demand more elastic.
• Snob effect (negative): you want it because few others have it → demand less elastic.

flashcards.question: How does the demand curve relate to utility maximization?
flashcards.answer: Each point on an individual demand curve is a utility-maximizing choice for that price. As price falls, the budget line pivots out and the optimum moves to a larger quantity — generating the downward-sloping demand curve.

flashcards.question: Why is market demand usually more elastic than individual demand?
flashcards.answer: A lower price keeps existing buyers buying more AND brings new buyers into the market. Summing many individuals’ responses makes total quantity more responsive to price.

learn.content:
Individual & Market Demand

The individual demand curve falls out of consumer theory: as a good’s price drops, the budget line pivots outward and the optimal basket moves to a larger quantity. Every point on the curve is a utility-maximizing choice.

Income changes and Engel curves

Tracing the optimum as INCOME changes gives the Engel curve (quantity vs. income). It rises for normal goods and falls for inferior goods.

Substitution & income effects

A price change has two parts: the substitution effect (the good is now relatively cheaper → buy more, always opposite the price change) and the income effect (real purchasing power changes). For a normal good both push the same way; for an inferior good the income effect opposes the substitution effect.

From individual to market demand

The market demand curve is the horizontal sum of all individuals’ demand curves — at each price, add up everyone’s quantity. More buyers and larger individual responses make it flatter (more elastic).

Consumer surplus & network effects

Consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price — the extra value buyers get beyond what they pay. Network externalities make one person’s demand depend on others’: the bandwagon effect (want it because others have it) and the snob effect (want it because few do).

Demand summarizes willingness to pay; supply will summarize willingness to sell — together they set the market price.

flashcards.question: Define probability, payoff, and expected value.
flashcards.answer:
• Probability — the likelihood a given outcome occurs.
• Payoff — the value associated with a possible outcome.
• Expected value — a probability-weighted average of the payoffs:
\( E(X) = \sum_i p_i x_i \)

flashcards.question: A job pays $1,500 with probability 0.5 and $500 with probability 0.5. What is the expected value?
flashcards.answer: \( E(X) = 0.5\times 1500 + 0.5\times 500 = 1000 \). (Reported in USD.)
flashcards.explanation: Expected value weights each payoff by its probability.

flashcards.question: What is variability, and how is it measured?
flashcards.answer:
Variability is the extent to which possible outcomes differ. It is measured by the variance (and its square root, the standard deviation):
\( \sigma^2 = \sum_i p_i\,(x_i - E(X))^2 \)

flashcards.question: What is expected utility?
flashcards.answer:
The sum of the utilities of all possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities:
\( E(U) = \sum_i p_i\,u(x_i) \).
People maximize expected UTILITY, not expected value.

flashcards.question: Distinguish risk-averse, risk-neutral, and risk-loving.
flashcards.answer:
Defined by the marginal utility of income:
• Risk averse — diminishing MU of income; prefers a sure thing to a fair gamble.
• Risk neutral — constant MU; judges a gamble only by its expected value.
• Risk loving — increasing MU; prefers the gamble.

flashcards.question: What is the risk premium?
flashcards.answer: The maximum amount of money a risk-averse person would pay (give up in expected value) to AVOID a risk — i.e. to make a risky prospect equivalent to a certain one.

flashcards.question: What are the three common ways to reduce risk?
flashcards.answer:
1. Diversification — spread across many (uncorrelated) choices
2. Insurance — pay a small certain premium to avoid a large uncertain loss
3. Obtaining more information about choices and payoffs

flashcards.question: Why are risk-averse people willing to buy insurance?
flashcards.answer: Because of diminishing marginal utility of income: the utility lost from paying a small certain premium is less than the expected utility lost from a possible large loss. A fairly priced policy raises their expected utility.

flashcards.question: What is the trade-off between risk and return on assets?
flashcards.answer: A riskless asset gives a certain return; a risky asset offers a higher EXPECTED return to compensate for its variability. Investors choose a mix according to how risk-averse they are.

learn.content:
Uncertainty & Consumer Behavior

When outcomes are uncertain we describe them with probabilities and payoffs. The single best summary of a risky prospect is its expected value — the probability-weighted average of payoffs:

\[ E(X) = \sum_i p_i\,x_i \]

Worked example — expected value

A sales job pays \(1{,}500\) with probability \(0.5\) and \(500\) with probability \(0.5\) (in USD).

\[ E(X) = 0.5\times 1500 + 0.5\times 500 = 1000 \]

So the expected income is 1,000 — even though neither outcome equals 1,000.

Risk, variability and utility

Two prospects can share an expected value but differ in variability, measured by the variance:

\[ \sigma^2 = \sum_i p_i\,(x_i - E(X))^2 \]

People actually maximize expected utility, \(E(U)=\sum_i p_i\,u(x_i)\). The shape of the utility-of-income function defines attitudes to risk:

  • Risk averse — diminishing marginal utility; prefers the sure thing
  • Risk neutral — constant MU; cares only about \(E(X)\)
  • Risk loving — increasing MU; prefers the gamble

Reducing risk

Risk-averse people lower risk by diversification (spreading across uncorrelated choices), insurance (a small certain premium instead of a large uncertain loss), and gathering more information. The most they will pay to avoid a risk is the risk premium.

Higher expected return on an asset typically comes only with higher risk — the risk-return trade-off.

flashcards.question: What three decisions make up the theory of the firm’s production?
flashcards.answer:
1. Production technology — how inputs turn into output
2. Cost constraints — the prices of labor, capital and other inputs
3. Input choices — how much of each input to use

flashcards.question: What is a production function?
flashcards.answer:
The relationship giving the MAXIMUM output obtainable from each combination of inputs, given the technology:
\( Q = F(K, L) \) (K = capital, L = labor).

flashcards.question: Short run vs. long run in production — what defines them?
flashcards.answer: The short run is a period in which at least one input is FIXED (often capital). In the long run ALL inputs are variable. They are defined by flexibility, not a fixed calendar length.

flashcards.question: Define average product and marginal product of labor.
flashcards.answer:
• Average product: output per worker, \(AP_L = \dfrac{Q}{L}\)
• Marginal product: extra output from one more worker, \(MP_L = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta L}\)

flashcards.question: State the law of diminishing marginal returns.
flashcards.answer: As more of a variable input (e.g. labor) is added to fixed inputs, beyond some point the marginal product of that input declines. It is about the short run, not about bad workers.

flashcards.question: What is the relationship between MP and AP curves?
flashcards.answer: When \(MP_L > AP_L\), average product is RISING; when \(MP_L < AP_L\), average product is FALLING. So \(MP_L\) crosses \(AP_L\) at the maximum of \(AP_L\).

flashcards.question: What is an isoquant?
flashcards.answer: A curve showing all combinations of two inputs (e.g. capital and labor) that yield the SAME output. An isoquant map shows several output levels.

flashcards.question: What is the marginal rate of technical substitution (MRTS)?
flashcards.answer:
The rate at which a firm can swap one input for another holding output constant — the magnitude of the isoquant’s slope:
\( MRTS = -\dfrac{\Delta K}{\Delta L} = \dfrac{MP_L}{MP_K} \).
It diminishes along an isoquant.

flashcards.question: Name the two special-case production functions.
flashcards.answer:
• Perfect substitutes — inputs replace each other at a constant rate (straight-line isoquants).
• Fixed proportions (Leontief) — inputs must be used in a fixed ratio (L-shaped isoquants).

flashcards.question: What are returns to scale?
flashcards.answer:
How output responds when ALL inputs are scaled up together:
• Increasing — output more than doubles when inputs double
• Constant — output exactly doubles
• Decreasing — output less than doubles

Two variable inputs

An isoquant shows the input combinations giving the same output. Its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution:

\[ MRTS = -\frac{\Delta K}{\Delta L} = \frac{MP_L}{MP_K} \]

Special cases: perfect substitutes (straight isoquants) and fixed proportions / Leontief (L-shaped).

Returns to scale describe scaling ALL inputs together: increasing, constant, or decreasing — distinct from diminishing returns to a single input in the short run.

flashcards.question: Economic cost vs. accounting cost — what is the difference?
flashcards.answer: Accounting cost counts explicit out-of-pocket expenses (and depreciation). Economic cost also includes the OPPORTUNITY cost of all resources — e.g. the salary the owner gives up, or the return on capital used in the business.

flashcards.question: What is opportunity cost, and what is a sunk cost?
flashcards.answer: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone when a resource is used. A sunk cost is an expenditure already made and unrecoverable — it should be IGNORED in current decisions.

flashcards.question: Distinguish fixed cost (FC) and variable cost (VC), and write total cost.
flashcards.answer:
Fixed cost does not change with output (paid even at \(Q=0\)); variable cost rises with output. Total cost is their sum:
\( TC = FC + VC \)

flashcards.question: Define marginal cost.
flashcards.answer:
The extra cost of producing one more unit:
\( MC = \dfrac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q} = \dfrac{\Delta VC}{\Delta Q} \) (since FC does not change).

flashcards.question: Write the three average cost measures.
flashcards.answer:
\( ATC = \dfrac{TC}{Q}, \quad AFC = \dfrac{FC}{Q}, \quad AVC = \dfrac{VC}{Q} \)
and they satisfy \( ATC = AFC + AVC \).

flashcards.question: How does the marginal cost curve relate to AVC and ATC?
flashcards.answer: MC cuts both AVC and ATC at their MINIMUM points. While \(MC<AVC\) average cost falls; while \(MC>AVC\) it rises. ATC and AVC are U-shaped.

flashcards.question: What happens to average fixed cost (AFC) as output rises?
flashcards.answer: AFC = FC/Q falls continuously as output rises (fixed cost is spread over more units) — the gap between ATC and AVC narrows.

flashcards.question: What is the cost-minimizing input rule in the long run?
flashcards.answer:
Choose inputs where the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line:
\( MRTS = \dfrac{w}{r} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \dfrac{MP_L}{w} = \dfrac{MP_K}{r} \)
(the marginal product per dollar is equal across inputs).

flashcards.question: Economies vs. diseconomies of scale — define them.
flashcards.answer:
• Economies of scale: long-run average cost FALLS as output rises (doubling output costs less than double).
• Diseconomies of scale: long-run average cost RISES with output (doubling output costs more than double).

flashcards.question: What are economies of scope and the learning curve?
flashcards.answer:
• Economies of scope: it is cheaper to produce several products together than separately.
• Learning curve: average cost falls as cumulative experience (output) grows — distinct from economies of scale.

learn.content:
The Cost of Production

Firms care about economic cost, which adds the opportunity cost of all resources (e.g. the owner’s forgone salary) to accounting cost. Sunk costs — already spent and unrecoverable — are irrelevant to decisions.

Short-run costs

Split total cost into fixed and variable parts, then derive the averages and the margin:

\[ TC = FC + VC, \qquad MC = \frac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q} = \frac{\Delta VC}{\Delta Q} \]
\[ ATC = \frac{TC}{Q}, \quad AFC = \frac{FC}{Q}, \quad AVC = \frac{VC}{Q}, \quad ATC = AFC + AVC \]

Worked example — cost measures

At \(Q = 10\): fixed cost \(FC = 100\), variable cost \(VC = 200\) (USD).

\[ TC = 100 + 200 = 300, \quad ATC = \frac{300}{10} = 30 \]
\[ AFC = \frac{100}{10} = 10, \qquad AVC = \frac{200}{10} = 20 \]

Check: \(AFC + AVC = 10 + 20 = 30 = ATC\). ✓

The marginal–average relationship

ATC and AVC are U-shaped, and MC cuts each at its minimum. While \(MC < AVC\) the average falls; once \(MC > AVC\) it rises. AFC falls continuously, so ATC and AVC converge as output grows.

Long-run costs

In the long run the firm picks the cheapest input mix where an isoquant is tangent to an isocost line:

\[ MRTS = \frac{w}{r} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{MP_L}{w} = \frac{MP_K}{r} \]

Long-run average cost shows economies of scale (falling), then constant, then diseconomies (rising); economies of scope and the learning curve lower costs further.

flashcards.question: How is profit defined, and what does a firm maximize?
flashcards.answer:
Profit is total revenue minus total cost:
\( \pi = TR - TC \)
The firm chooses the output level that makes this difference as large as possible.

flashcards.question: State the profit-maximizing rule for any firm.
flashcards.answer:
Produce the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost:
\( MR = MC \)
If \(MR > MC\), producing more adds to profit; if \(MR < MC\), cutting output raises profit.

flashcards.question: Why is a perfectly competitive firm a "price taker", and what does that imply for MR?
flashcards.answer:
It is one of many sellers of a homogeneous product, so it cannot influence the market price — it faces a horizontal (infinitely elastic) demand curve at the market price. Therefore price equals average and marginal revenue:
\( P = AR = MR \)
so the profit-max condition becomes \( P = MR = MC \).

flashcards.question: List the four market structures.
flashcards.answer:
1. Perfect competition — many firms, homogeneous product
2. Monopoly — a single seller
3. Monopolistic competition — many firms, DIFFERENTIATED products, free entry
4. Oligopoly — a few firms, entry possible but not easy

flashcards.question: What are the defining characteristics of perfect competition?
flashcards.answer:
• A great number of buyers and sellers
• A homogeneous (identical) product
• Perfect mobility of resources
• Perfect knowledge of present and future prices, costs and opportunities
Each firm is a price taker.

flashcards.question: What is the short-run shut-down rule?
flashcards.answer: A competitive firm keeps producing as long as price covers average variable cost (\(P \ge AVC\)). If \(P < AVC\) it shuts down, because it would lose less by producing nothing (it still pays fixed cost either way).

flashcards.question: What is the short-run supply curve of a competitive firm?
flashcards.answer: The rising portion of its marginal cost curve that lies ABOVE the average variable cost curve. Below the minimum of AVC the firm supplies zero (shut-down).

flashcards.question: Distinguish producer surplus from profit.
flashcards.answer: Producer surplus is the sum, over all units, of the difference between price and marginal cost (price minus variable cost) — it is revenue minus VARIABLE cost. Profit is revenue minus TOTAL cost. They differ by fixed cost: producer surplus exceeds profit by the amount of fixed cost.

flashcards.question: What conditions hold in long-run competitive equilibrium?
flashcards.answer:
1. Every firm maximizes profit (\(P = MR = MC\)).
2. No firm has an incentive to enter or exit — economic profit is ZERO.
3. The price clears the market (quantity supplied = quantity demanded).
Firms produce at the lowest point of their long-run average cost curve: \( P = MR = LMC = \min(LAC) \).

flashcards.question: Why is long-run economic profit zero in perfect competition?
flashcards.answer: Free entry: if firms earn positive economic profit, new firms enter, supply rises and price falls until profit is competed away to zero. Losses cause exit, raising price back to break-even. Zero ECONOMIC profit still means a normal return on resources.

flashcards.question: What is economic rent?
flashcards.answer: The amount firms are willing to pay for an input ABOVE the minimum amount needed to obtain it (its opportunity cost). It arises for inputs in fixed/limited supply (e.g. especially productive land).

learn.content:
Profit Maximization & Competitive Supply

A firm maximizes profit, the gap between revenue and cost:

\[ \pi = TR - TC \]

Profit is largest at the output where the last unit just pays for itself — where marginal revenue equals marginal cost:

\[ MR = MC \]

The competitive firm is a price taker

Under perfect competition there are many sellers of a homogeneous product, so a single firm cannot move the price. It faces a horizontal demand curve at the market price, which makes price, average revenue and marginal revenue all equal:

\[ P = AR = MR \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P = MR = MC \]

Worked example — choosing output

The market price is \(P = 20\) (USD) and the firm’s marginal cost is \(MC = 2Q\).

\[ P = MC \;\Rightarrow\; 20 = 2Q \;\Rightarrow\; Q = 10 \]

The firm supplies 10 units. If the price rose to 30, it would produce where \(30 = 2Q\), i.e. \(Q = 15\) — tracing out its supply curve along MC.

Shut-down rule & the supply curve

In the short run the firm produces only if price covers average variable cost (\(P \ge AVC\)); otherwise it shuts down and loses just its fixed cost. Its short-run supply curve is therefore the part of MC lying above minimum AVC.

The long run: zero economic profit

With free entry and exit, positive profit attracts new firms (raising supply, lowering price) and losses drive firms out, until profit is competed away. In equilibrium every firm sits at the bottom of its long-run average cost curve:

\[ P = MR = LMC = \min(LAC), \qquad \pi = 0 \]

Zero economic profit still means a normal (competitive) return; inputs in fixed supply earn economic rent — payment above their opportunity cost.

flashcards.question: What are consumer surplus and producer surplus?
flashcards.answer: Consumer surplus is the difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay (area under the demand curve, above the price). Producer surplus is the difference between the price received and the minimum suppliers would accept (area above the supply curve, below the price).

flashcards.question: What is deadweight loss?
flashcards.answer: The net loss of total surplus (consumer + producer) caused by a market distortion — such as a price control, tax, quota or monopoly — that moves output away from the competitive equilibrium quantity. It represents mutually beneficial trades that no longer happen.

flashcards.question: What does a price ceiling (below equilibrium) do?
flashcards.answer: A binding price ceiling holds price BELOW the market-clearing level → quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (a SHORTAGE). Consumers who still buy gain, but the reduced quantity creates a deadweight loss.

flashcards.question: What does a price floor / price support (above equilibrium) do?
flashcards.answer: A binding price floor holds price ABOVE the market-clearing level → quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded (a SURPLUS). A minimum wage and agricultural price supports are examples; they also create deadweight loss (and, with supports, a government purchase cost).

flashcards.question: When is a competitive market economically efficient, and what is market failure?
flashcards.answer: A competitive market maximizes the sum of consumer and producer surplus, so it is efficient. MARKET FAILURE occurs when unregulated markets are inefficient — chiefly because of externalities or a lack of information.

flashcards.question: What is a specific tax, and who bears its burden (tax incidence)?
flashcards.answer: A specific tax is a fixed amount of money per unit sold. The INCIDENCE (who actually bears it) does not depend on who legally pays it — it falls more heavily on the side of the market that is LESS elastic (more inelastic). The tax also creates a deadweight loss.

flashcards.question: How does relative elasticity determine who bears a tax?
flashcards.answer: The more INELASTIC side bears the larger share. If demand is more inelastic than supply, buyers pay most of the tax (price rises a lot); if supply is more inelastic, sellers absorb most of it.

flashcards.question: What is the effect of a production quota or import quota?
flashcards.answer: A quota restricts the quantity that may be produced or imported, pushing price up. Consumers lose surplus; domestic producers (or quota/license holders) gain; the restriction on quantity creates a deadweight loss.

flashcards.question: What is the effect of a subsidy?
flashcards.answer: A subsidy is a negative tax — a payment per unit that lowers the price buyers pay and raises the price sellers receive, increasing the quantity traded ABOVE the efficient level. It too generates a deadweight loss (and a government cost) because output exceeds the efficient amount.

flashcards.question: What is an import tariff?
flashcards.answer: A tax on imported goods. It raises the domestic price toward (or above) the world-price-plus-tariff, reducing imports. Domestic producers and the government (tariff revenue) gain, consumers lose more, and there is a deadweight loss.

learn.content:
The Analysis of Competitive Markets

We measure the well-being of a market with consumer surplus (value to buyers above the price they pay) and producer surplus (price received above the seller’s minimum). A competitive equilibrium maximizes their sum, so it is efficient.

Worked example — consumer surplus

Demand is \(P = 100 - Q\) and the equilibrium price is \(P = 40\), so quantity is \(Q = 60\). Consumer surplus is the triangle between the demand curve and the price:

\[ CS = \tfrac{1}{2}\,(100 - 40)\times 60 = \tfrac{1}{2}\times 60 \times 60 = 1800 \]

(in USD). Anything that pushes quantity below 60 sacrifices some of this surplus.

Price controls

A binding price ceiling (below equilibrium) causes a shortage; a binding price floor (above equilibrium, e.g. a minimum wage or farm price support) causes a surplus. Either way the quantity traded falls below the efficient level, producing a deadweight loss.

Tax incidence depends on elasticity

A specific tax (a fixed amount per unit) raises the price buyers pay and lowers the price sellers receive. Who really bears it does not depend on who writes the cheque — the more inelastic side of the market bears the larger share. A subsidy works in reverse, pushing output ABOVE the efficient level.

Quotas, tariffs, supports, taxes and subsidies all move quantity away from the competitive equilibrium and so create deadweight loss — they redistribute surplus at a cost to total welfare. Markets fail on their own mainly because of externalities and missing information.

flashcards.question: What is a monopoly, and why is its marginal revenue below price?
flashcards.answer:
A monopoly is the single seller of a product with no close substitutes; it faces the entire downward-sloping market demand curve. To sell one more unit it must lower the price on ALL units, so marginal revenue is less than price:
\( MR < P \).

flashcards.question: For a linear demand curve, how does the MR curve relate to the demand curve?
flashcards.answer:
The marginal revenue curve has the same intercept but is TWICE as steep. If demand is \(P = a - bQ\), then
\( MR = a - 2bQ \)
(the absolute slope of MR is double that of demand).

flashcards.question: How does a monopolist choose output and price?
flashcards.answer: It sets output where \(MR = MC\), then charges the highest price the demand curve allows for that quantity. Because \(MR < P\), the monopoly produces LESS and charges MORE than a competitive industry would.

flashcards.question: What is the Lerner index of monopoly power?
flashcards.answer:
A measure of markup over marginal cost:
\( L = \dfrac{P - MC}{P} = -\dfrac{1}{E_d} \)
It ranges from 0 (price taker) toward 1; the more inelastic the demand the firm faces, the greater its monopoly power.

flashcards.question: What are the sources of monopoly power?
flashcards.answer:
1. The elasticity of market demand (less elastic → more power)
2. The number of firms in the market (fewer → more power; barriers to entry)
3. The interaction among firms (more rivalrous → less power)

flashcards.question: What are the social costs of monopoly power?
flashcards.answer: A monopoly restricts output below the efficient level, creating a DEADWEIGHT LOSS (lost consumer and producer surplus). Firms may also spend resources to gain or keep monopoly power — RENT SEEKING — which wastes resources. Price regulation can reduce the loss.

flashcards.question: What is a natural monopoly, and how is it often regulated?
flashcards.answer: A natural monopoly has economies of scale so large that one firm can serve the whole market at lower cost than several could (e.g. water, electricity grids). It is often regulated by setting a price (e.g. rate-of-return regulation) closer to average or marginal cost.

flashcards.question: What is monopsony (and monopsony power)?
flashcards.answer: Monopsony is a market with a single BUYER (oligopsony = a few buyers). Monopsony power is a buyer’s ability to affect the price it pays. The buyer faces an upward-sloping supply curve, so its marginal expenditure exceeds the average expenditure (price).

flashcards.question: What is the monopsonist’s purchasing rule?
flashcards.answer:
It buys up to the point where the marginal VALUE of the input equals the marginal EXPENDITURE:
\( MV = ME \)
Because \(ME > \) price, the monopsonist buys LESS and pays a LOWER price than a competitive buyer would.

flashcards.question: What are the sources of monopsony power?
flashcards.answer:
1. The elasticity of market supply (less elastic → more power)
2. The number of buyers (fewer → more power)
3. The interaction among buyers

flashcards.question: How do antitrust laws limit market power?
flashcards.answer: They prohibit anticompetitive behavior — e.g. agreements to fix prices or restrict output (parallel conduct / collusion) and predatory pricing aimed at driving out rivals — and restrict mergers that would create excessive market power.

learn.content:
Market Power: Monopoly & Monopsony

A monopoly is the only seller, so it faces the whole downward-sloping demand curve. To sell one more unit it must cut the price on every unit, which is why marginal revenue lies below price. For a linear demand the MR curve shares the intercept but is twice as steep:

\[ P = a - bQ \quad\Longrightarrow\quad MR = a - 2bQ \]

Worked example — monopoly output and price

Demand: \(P = 100 - Q\); marginal cost: \(MC = 20\) (USD). Then \(MR = 100 - 2Q\). Set \(MR = MC\):

\[ 100 - 2Q = 20 \;\Rightarrow\; Q = 40, \qquad P = 100 - 40 = 60 \]

A competitive industry would set \(P = MC = 20\) and \(Q = 80\). The monopoly produces half as much at three times the price — the gap is deadweight loss. Its markup gives a Lerner index \(L = (60-20)/60 \approx 0.67\).

Measuring and sourcing market power

The Lerner index ties the markup to the elasticity of demand the firm faces:

\[ L = \frac{P - MC}{P} = -\frac{1}{E_d} \]

Power grows with inelastic demand, few firms (barriers to entry) and less aggressive rivalry.

Monopsony — power on the buying side

A monopsony is a single buyer facing an upward-sloping supply curve, so its marginal expenditure exceeds the price. It buys where \(MV = ME\), purchasing less and paying less than a competitive buyer. Antitrust laws limit both monopoly and monopsony power by banning price fixing, predatory pricing and anticompetitive mergers.

Because a monopoly sets \(MR = MC\) while the efficient rule is \(P = MC\), it restricts output and creates a deadweight loss; natural monopolies (huge economies of scale) are usually price-regulated instead of broken up.

flashcards.question: What defines monopolistic competition?
flashcards.answer: Many firms selling DIFFERENTIATED products, with free entry and exit. Each firm has a little market power over its own variety (so it faces a downward-sloping demand and sets price), but free entry drives long-run economic profit to zero.

flashcards.question: What can a monopolistically competitive firm choose?
flashcards.answer: The characteristics of its product, its selling/advertising expenses, and the price and quantity of its product — because product differentiation gives it some pricing discretion.

flashcards.question: Why is monopolistic competition not fully efficient in the long run?
flashcards.answer: In long-run equilibrium price equals average cost (zero profit), but production occurs where \(P > MC\) and NOT at the minimum of average cost. The firm operates with EXCESS CAPACITY, so there is a small efficiency loss — the price of product variety.

flashcards.question: What defines an oligopoly?
flashcards.answer: A few firms account for most or all production; the product may or may not be differentiated; there are barriers to entry, so firms can earn long-run profit. Each firm’s best action depends on what rivals do — they are INTERDEPENDENT.

flashcards.question: What is a Nash equilibrium?
flashcards.answer: A set of strategies (one per firm) in which each firm is doing the best it can GIVEN what its competitors are doing — so no firm wants to change its choice unilaterally.

flashcards.question: What is the Cournot model?
flashcards.answer: An oligopoly model where firms compete by choosing QUANTITIES simultaneously, each taking the other’s output as given. Each firm’s reaction curve shows its best output given the rival’s; the Cournot equilibrium is where the reaction curves intersect (a Nash equilibrium in quantities).

flashcards.question: What is the Stackelberg model?
flashcards.answer: A quantity-setting oligopoly where one firm moves FIRST (the leader) and the other responds (the follower). The leader gains a first-mover advantage, producing more and earning more than the follower.

flashcards.question: What is the Bertrand model?
flashcards.answer: An oligopoly model where firms compete by setting PRICES (rather than quantities). With identical products, price competition drives price down to marginal cost — even with only two firms — so profits are competed away.

flashcards.question: What is the prisoners’ dilemma, and how does it apply to oligopoly?
flashcards.answer: A non-cooperative game in which each player’s dominant strategy leads to an outcome that is worse for BOTH than if they had cooperated. In oligopoly, firms would jointly profit by keeping prices high, but each has an incentive to undercut — so they often end up in a low-price (competitive-like) outcome.

flashcards.question: What are kinked demand and price leadership?
flashcards.answer: The KINKED demand curve model explains price RIGIDITY: rivals match price cuts but not price rises, so demand is more elastic above the current price than below it, discouraging changes. PRICE LEADERSHIP (e.g. a dominant firm) is a way firms coordinate prices without explicit collusion.

flashcards.question: What is a cartel?
flashcards.answer: A group of producers that EXPLICITLY agree to cooperate in setting prices and output (acting like a monopoly). Examples: OPEC (oil), CIPEC (copper). Cartels are unstable because each member is tempted to cheat by producing more.

learn.content:
Monopolistic Competition & Oligopoly

Monopolistic competition mixes both worlds: many firms, but each sells a differentiated product, giving it a downward-sloping demand and some pricing power. Free entry still drives long-run profit to zero — yet the firm ends up producing where \(P > MC\) and not at minimum average cost, leaving excess capacity. That small inefficiency is the price we pay for product variety.

Oligopoly: a few interdependent firms

In an oligopoly a handful of firms supply the market, protected by barriers to entry. Because each firm’s best move depends on its rivals’, we use game theory. The key solution concept is the Nash equilibrium: a set of strategies where no firm can do better by changing its own choice alone.

Quantity vs. price competition

• Cournot: firms choose QUANTITIES simultaneously; equilibrium is where their reaction curves cross.
• Stackelberg: one firm chooses quantity FIRST and gains a first-mover advantage.
• Bertrand: firms choose PRICES; with identical products price is driven down to marginal cost.

The prisoners’ dilemma

Two firms each choose a HIGH or LOW price. Both would earn more if both kept prices high, but each has a dominant incentive to undercut. Acting in self-interest, both cut → the (Low, Low) outcome, worse for both than cooperation. This is why cartels (OPEC, CIPEC) are unstable: every member is tempted to cheat.

Without explicit collusion, firms may still coordinate through price leadership or the kinked demand curve, which keeps prices rigid because rivals match cuts but not increases.

flashcards.question: What is a "game" in game theory, and what are payoffs and strategies?
flashcards.answer: A game is any situation in which players make strategic decisions that take account of one another’s actions. PAYOFFS are the outcomes (rewards) that result; a STRATEGY is a rule or plan of action for playing the game; an OPTIMAL strategy maximizes a player’s expected payoff.

flashcards.question: Cooperative vs. non-cooperative games — what is the difference?
flashcards.answer: In a COOPERATIVE game players can negotiate binding contracts that let them plan joint strategies. In a NON-COOPERATIVE game binding agreements are not possible, so each player acts in its own interest. Most strategic interaction in markets is non-cooperative.

flashcards.question: What is a dominant strategy?
flashcards.answer: A strategy that is optimal NO MATTER what the opponent does. When every player has a dominant strategy, the outcome is an equilibrium in dominant strategies — a particularly strong prediction.

flashcards.question: What is a Nash equilibrium (in game-theory terms)?
flashcards.answer: A set of strategies in which each player chooses the best response to the others’ strategies, so no player can improve by changing its own strategy alone. Every dominant-strategy equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium, but not vice versa.

flashcards.question: What is a maximin strategy?
flashcards.answer: A cautious (risk-averse) strategy that maximizes the player’s MINIMUM possible payoff — it guards against the worst case rather than maximizing the expected payoff. Useful when a player is uncertain or doubts the rationality of the rival.

flashcards.question: What is a mixed strategy?
flashcards.answer: A strategy in which a player makes a random choice among two or more possible actions, according to set probabilities. Some games have no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium but do have one in mixed strategies.

flashcards.question: What is a repeated game, and what is tit-for-tat?
flashcards.answer: A repeated game is one in which actions are taken and payoffs received over and over. TIT-FOR-TAT is a strategy of cooperating first, then doing whatever the opponent did last period. In infinitely (or indefinitely) repeated games, tit-for-tat can sustain cooperation that a one-shot game cannot.

flashcards.question: What is a sequential game and the advantage of moving first?
flashcards.answer: A sequential game is one in which players move in TURN, responding to each other’s actions (drawn in EXTENSIVE form, a tree). Moving first can be an advantage: a credible commitment by the first mover can shape the rival’s best response in its favor.

flashcards.question: Why must threats and commitments be credible?
flashcards.answer: An EMPTY threat — one it would not be in the player’s interest to carry out — does not influence rivals. To matter, a threat or commitment must be CREDIBLE; building a reputation, or making an irreversible commitment, makes it so.

flashcards.question: What is entry deterrence?
flashcards.answer: Actions by an incumbent that convince a potential competitor that entering would be unprofitable — e.g. a credible commitment to expand capacity or fight a price war. The threat must be credible (backed by a real commitment) to deter entry.

flashcards.question: What is the winner’s curse in auctions?
flashcards.answer: In a common-value auction (the item is worth roughly the same to all bidders but its value is uncertain), the winner tends to be the one who most OVERESTIMATED the value — so winning often means having overpaid. Rational bidders shade their bids to avoid this.

learn.content:
Game Theory & Competitive Strategy

A game is any situation in which players make strategic decisions, anticipating one another. Each player has strategies (plans of action) leading to payoffs; an optimal strategy maximizes a player’s expected payoff. In non-cooperative games binding agreements are impossible, so each acts in self-interest.

Solution concepts

• A dominant strategy is best no matter what the rival does.
• A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where each player best-responds to the others — no one wants to deviate alone.
• A maximin strategy maximizes the worst-case payoff (cautious play).
• A mixed strategy randomizes over actions when no pure equilibrium exists.

Worked example — dominant strategy

Two firms set price High or Low. Profits (Firm 1, Firm 2):

(High, High) = (10, 10)  ·  (High, Low) = (2, 14)
(Low, High) = (14, 2)  ·  (Low, Low) = (5, 5)

Whatever the rival does, each firm earns more by choosing Low (14 > 10, 5 > 2). Low is a dominant strategy, so the Nash equilibrium is (Low, Low) = (5, 5) — worse for both than (High, High). That is the prisoners’ dilemma.

Repetition, sequence and credibility

In repeated games, tit-for-tat can sustain cooperation that a one-shot game cannot. In sequential games (extensive form) moving first can pay — but only a credible threat or commitment (backed by reputation or an irreversible move) changes a rival’s behavior; an empty threat is ignored.

Applications include entry deterrence, bargaining, and auctions — where the winner’s curse warns bidders in common-value auctions to shade their bids.

flashcards.question: What does it mean that the demand for a factor of production is a "derived" demand?
flashcards.answer: Demand for an input (labor, capital, land) is DERIVED from the demand for the output it helps produce. A firm hires an input not for its own sake but because it contributes to producing a good that can be sold.

flashcards.question: What is the marginal revenue product of labor (MRP_L)?
flashcards.answer:
The extra revenue from hiring one more unit of labor:
\( MRP_L = MR \times MP_L \)
In a competitive OUTPUT market \(MR = P\), so
\( MRP_L = P \times MP_L \).

flashcards.question: How much labor does a firm in a competitive factor market hire?
flashcards.answer:
It hires up to the point where the marginal revenue product equals the wage (the price of labor):
\( MRP_L = w \)
Hiring more would cost more than it adds; hiring less would forgo profitable output.

flashcards.question: What are average expenditure and marginal expenditure on an input?
flashcards.answer: Average expenditure is the price paid per unit of the input (the input supply curve). Marginal expenditure is the extra cost of buying one more unit. For a COMPETITIVE buyer they are equal (the input price); for a MONOPSONIST, marginal expenditure EXCEEDS average expenditure.

flashcards.question: What is the backward-bending supply curve of labor?
flashcards.answer: At low wages, a wage rise increases hours worked (substitution effect dominates — leisure is more expensive). At high wages, the income effect can dominate: workers feel richer and "buy" more leisure, so hours worked FALL — the supply curve bends backward.

flashcards.question: Explain the substitution and income effects of a wage increase.
flashcards.answer: SUBSTITUTION effect: a higher wage makes leisure more expensive, so the worker substitutes toward work (more hours). INCOME effect: the higher wage makes the worker richer, encouraging more leisure (fewer hours). The net effect determines the slope of labor supply.

flashcards.question: What is economic rent in a factor market?
flashcards.answer: The payment to a factor above the minimum needed to keep it in its current use (above its opportunity cost / supply price). LAND RENT is the classic case: land is in fixed supply, so all payment to it is economic rent.

flashcards.question: How does a monopsony buy a factor input, and what is the rule?
flashcards.answer: A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping input supply curve, so its marginal expenditure exceeds the price. It maximizes net benefit by buying up to where marginal value equals marginal expenditure (\(MV = ME\)); since \(MV = MRP\) for a firm, the rule is \(ME = MRP\). It hires LESS and pays a LOWER wage than a competitive buyer.

flashcards.question: How does monopoly power in a factor market (e.g. a union) affect wages?
flashcards.answer: A seller of labor with monopoly power (such as a labor union) can raise the wage above the competitive level, but at the cost of fewer jobs (lower quantity of labor employed) — a trade-off between the wage rate and the number employed.

flashcards.question: What is equilibrium in a competitive factor market?
flashcards.answer: It occurs where the market demand for the input (the sum of firms’ MRP curves) equals the market supply of the input. There the input price (e.g. the wage) and the quantity employed are determined, and every firm hires until \(MRP = \) input price.

learn.content:
Markets for Factor Inputs

Firms buy inputs — labor, capital, land — so the demand for a factor is a derived demand: it comes from the demand for the output the factor helps produce. The value of one more worker is the marginal revenue product:

\[ MRP_L = MR \times MP_L \quad\xrightarrow{\text{competitive output}}\quad MRP_L = P \times MP_L \]

Worked example — the hiring rule

Output sells at \(P = 10\) (USD) and the next worker’s marginal product is \(MP_L = 5\) units. Then

\[ MRP_L = 10 \times 5 = 50 \]

A competitive firm hires until \(MRP_L = w\). If the wage is \(w = 50\) it is worth hiring this worker; if the wage were 60 it would not.

Average vs. marginal expenditure

A competitive buyer pays the same price for every unit, so marginal expenditure equals the price. A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping supply curve — buying more raises the price on all units — so its marginal expenditure EXCEEDS the price. It buys where \(MV = ME\) (i.e. \(ME = MRP\)), hiring less and paying less than a competitive buyer.

Labor supply and rent

A wage rise has two effects: the substitution effect (work more, leisure is dearer) and the income effect (work less, you feel richer). When income wins at high wages the labor supply curve bends backward.

Payment to a factor above its opportunity cost is economic rent — and because land is fixed in supply, all payment to land is rent. Unions (monopoly power in selling labor) can raise wages, but usually at the cost of fewer jobs.

flashcards.question: What is an externality?
flashcards.answer: A cost or benefit of an activity that falls on a THIRD party not involved in the transaction, and is not reflected in the market price. It can be NEGATIVE (e.g. pollution) or POSITIVE (e.g. a neighbor’s nice garden, or education).

flashcards.question: Why do negative externalities cause inefficiency?
flashcards.answer: The producer ignores the external cost, so the private marginal cost is below the marginal SOCIAL cost. The market therefore produces TOO MUCH of the good (output beyond the efficient level), creating a deadweight loss.

flashcards.question: Define marginal external cost and marginal social cost.
flashcards.answer:
Marginal external cost (MEC) is the cost imposed on third parties by one more unit. Marginal social cost is the private marginal cost plus that external cost:
\( MSC = MC + MEC \)
The efficient output is where \(MSC = MSB\) (marginal social benefit).

flashcards.question: Why do positive externalities also cause inefficiency?
flashcards.answer: When an activity confers external BENEFITS, the marginal social benefit exceeds the private benefit, so the market produces TOO LITTLE of the good (output below the efficient level). A subsidy can correct it.

flashcards.question: What is an emissions fee (a Pigouvian tax)?
flashcards.answer: A charge per unit of pollution emitted, set equal to the marginal external cost at the efficient level. It makes firms internalize the external cost (private cost rises to social cost), so they cut output/emissions to the efficient amount.

flashcards.question: Compare an emissions standard with an emissions fee.
flashcards.answer: A STANDARD sets a legal limit on emissions (a quantity); a FEE charges per unit emitted (a price). With uncertainty about firms’ abatement costs, the two are NOT equivalent — fees are usually cheaper when abatement costs vary across firms because they let low-cost abaters cut the most.

flashcards.question: What are tradeable emissions permits?
flashcards.answer: A system in which the government issues a fixed number of permits (a cap) that firms can BUY and SELL. Firms that can cut emissions cheaply sell permits to those for whom cutting is costly, so the total reduction is achieved at the LOWEST overall cost (cap-and-trade).

flashcards.question: What is the Coase theorem?
flashcards.answer: If property rights are clearly defined and bargaining is costless, private parties can negotiate an EFFICIENT outcome to an externality on their own, regardless of who holds the rights. In practice high transaction costs (and many parties) often prevent this.

flashcards.question: What is the common property resource problem?
flashcards.answer: A common property resource is one to which everyone has FREE access (e.g. ocean fisheries, common grazing land). Because no one owns it, each user ignores the cost imposed on others, so it is OVERUSED and depleted — the "tragedy of the commons".

flashcards.question: What defines a public good?
flashcards.answer: A good that is NONRIVAL (one person’s use does not reduce the amount available to others) and NONEXCLUSIVE (you cannot prevent non-payers from consuming it), e.g. national defense or clean air. These features lead to the FREE-RIDER problem.

flashcards.question: What is the free-rider problem?
flashcards.answer: Because a public good is nonexclusive, people can enjoy it without paying — so each has an incentive to "free ride" on others. As a result the private market under-provides public goods, which is why government often supplies them.

learn.content:
Externalities & Public Goods

An externality is a cost or benefit that spills onto a third party and is not in the price. With a negative externality (pollution) the firm ignores the harm, so private cost understates the true social cost and the market overproduces. The efficient rule compares full social cost and benefit:

\[ MSC = MC + MEC, \qquad \text{efficient where } MSC = MSB \]

Worked example — pricing the externality

A factory’s private marginal cost is \(MC = 10\) and each unit imposes a marginal external cost \(MEC = 4\) (USD). Then

\[ MSC = 10 + 4 = 14 \]

A Pigouvian fee of 4 per unit makes the firm face the full cost of 14, so it cuts output back to the efficient level where \(MSC = MSB\). A positive externality is corrected the opposite way — with a subsidy, because the market otherwise underproduces.

Standards, fees and permits

Government can set an emissions standard (a quantity limit), an emissions fee (a price per unit), or issue tradeable permits (cap-and-trade). Permits and fees reach a target at lowest cost because low-cost abaters cut the most. By the Coase theorem, clear property rights plus costless bargaining can fix an externality privately — but high transaction costs usually get in the way.

Common resources and public goods

Common property resources (open-access fisheries, grazing land) are overused — the tragedy of the commons. Public goods are nonrival and nonexclusive (national defense, clean air); their nonexcludability creates the free-rider problem.

Because free riders will not pay, private markets under-provide public goods — a key reason government finances them.

flashcards.question: What single idea unifies almost every optimization in microeconomics?
flashcards.answer:
"Optimize at the margin" — keep doing an activity until its marginal benefit equals its marginal cost. Each topic is one version of that rule:
\( MR = MC \) (profit), \( MRS = \dfrac{P_x}{P_y} \) (consumer), \( MRTS = \dfrac{w}{r} \) (cost-min), \( MRP_L = w \) (hiring), \( MSC = MSB \) (social efficiency).
flashcards.explanation: If MB > MC, do more; if MB < MC, do less. Equality = optimum.

flashcards.question: Summarize the four market structures (firms, product, entry, price vs MC, long-run profit).
flashcards.answer:
• Perfect competition: many firms, homogeneous, free entry, \(P = MC\), zero LR profit.
• Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated, free entry, \(P > MC\), zero LR profit (excess capacity).
• Oligopoly: a few interdependent firms, barriers, \(P > MC\), possible LR profit.
• Monopoly: one firm, no substitutes, blocked entry, \(P > MC\), LR profit persists.

flashcards.question: How is the consumer optimum characterized in two equivalent ways?
flashcards.answer:
At the best affordable basket the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line:
\( MRS = \dfrac{P_x}{P_y} \)
equivalently, the marginal utility per dollar is equal across all goods:
\( \dfrac{MU_x}{P_x} = \dfrac{MU_y}{P_y} \) (the equal-marginal principle).

flashcards.question: Define price elasticity of demand and its link to revenue and monopoly markup.
flashcards.answer: \( E_p = \dfrac{\%\,\Delta Q}{\%\,\Delta P} \). Demand is elastic if \(|E_p|>1\) (a price cut RAISES revenue), inelastic if \(|E_p|<1\) (a price cut LOWERS revenue). Monopoly markup is tied to it through the Lerner index: \( \dfrac{P-MC}{P} = -\dfrac{1}{E_d} \).

flashcards.question: Where does deadweight loss appear, and what is the common cause?
flashcards.answer: In monopoly, taxes/subsidies, price controls, quotas/tariffs, and externalities. The common cause is always the same: output moves AWAY from the efficient level (where \(P = MC\) for private goods, or \(MSC = MSB\) with externalities), so mutually beneficial trades are lost.

flashcards.question: Contrast diminishing marginal returns with returns to scale.
flashcards.answer: Diminishing marginal returns is a SHORT-RUN idea: adding more of ONE variable input (with others fixed) eventually raises output by less and less. Returns to scale is a LONG-RUN idea: scaling ALL inputs by the same factor — output may rise more than (increasing), equal to (constant) or less than (decreasing) proportionally.

flashcards.question: State the firm’s short-run produce/shut-down rule and the long-run entry/exit rule.
flashcards.answer: Short run: produce where \(MR = MC\), but shut down if \(P < AVC\) (then lose only fixed cost). Long run: exit if \(P < ATC\); under perfect competition free entry/exit drives \(P\) to \(\min(ATC)\) and economic profit to zero.

flashcards.question: How does a monopoly’s choice differ from a competitive firm’s, and why is it inefficient?
flashcards.answer: Both set \(MR = MC\), but for a competitive firm \(P = MR\), so \(P = MC\); for a monopoly \(MR < P\), so it stops where \(P > MC\). Producing where \(P>MC\) means some units worth more than they cost are not made → deadweight loss.

flashcards.question: Recap the economics of risk: expected value and attitudes to risk.
flashcards.answer: Expected value is the probability-weighted average payoff, \( E(X) = \sum p_i x_i \). A risk-AVERSE person prefers a sure thing to a fair gamble of equal expected value (diminishing marginal utility of wealth); risk-NEUTRAL is indifferent; risk-LOVING prefers the gamble. Risk is reduced by diversification, insurance and more information.

flashcards.question: How does a firm decide how much labor to hire, in competition and under monopsony?
flashcards.answer: Competitive factor market: hire until \(MRP_L = w\), where \(MRP_L = P \times MP_L\). Monopsony (single buyer): the supply curve slopes up so marginal expenditure exceeds the wage — hire until \(MV = ME\) (i.e. \(MRP = ME\)), employing less and paying less.

flashcards.question: List the toolkit for correcting externalities.
flashcards.answer: For NEGATIVE externalities (over-production): a Pigouvian fee/tax equal to the marginal external cost, an emissions standard, or tradeable permits (cap-and-trade); private Coasean bargaining if property rights are clear and transaction costs low. For POSITIVE externalities (under-production): a subsidy.

flashcards.question: Why do private markets under-provide public goods?
flashcards.answer: Public goods are NONRIVAL (one person’s use does not reduce others’) and NONEXCLUSIVE (non-payers cannot be shut out). Nonexclusivity creates the FREE-RIDER problem: each person hopes others will pay, so too little is funded — which is why government often provides them.

Final Exam Roadmap — the whole of micro on one page

The course tells one story: scarce resources are allocated by people and firms optimizing at the margin and by prices coordinating them. Drill the per-chapter categories in this lesson, then use this set to link them.

\[ \begin{aligned}\text{Consumer optimum:}\quad & MRS = \frac{P_x}{P_y}\;\Leftrightarrow\;\frac{MU_x}{P_x}=\frac{MU_y}{P_y}\\[2pt]\text{Cost minimization:}\quad & MRTS = \frac{w}{r}\\[2pt]\text{Profit maximization:}\quad & MR = MC\\[2pt]\text{Perfect competition:}\quad & P = MR = MC = \min(LAC)\\[2pt]\text{Monopoly markup:}\quad & \frac{P-MC}{P} = -\frac{1}{E_d}\\[2pt]\text{Hiring an input:}\quad & MRP_L = w \;\; (\text{monopsony: } MV = ME)\\[2pt]\text{Social efficiency:}\quad & MSC = MSB\end{aligned} \]

First midterm (Ch 1–7)

  • Preliminaries & supply–demand: scarcity, PPF, equilibrium; \(E_p = \%\Delta Q / \%\Delta P\), elastic vs inelastic and revenue.
  • Consumer behavior & demand: preferences, budget line, \(MRS = P_x/P_y\); income/substitution effects, consumer surplus.
  • Uncertainty: expected value \(E(X)=\sum p_i x_i\), risk attitudes, diversification/insurance.
  • Production & cost: \(MP\), \(MRTS\), returns to scale; \(TC = FC + VC\), \(MC = \Delta TC/\Delta Q\), U-shaped ATC/AVC.

Exam strategy

Closed questions reward exact conditions and formulas (\(MR=MC\), \(MRS=P_x/P_y\), Lerner index, \(MSC=MSB\)). Open questions reward concept + example (e.g. "negative externality → a factory’s pollution; fix with a Pigouvian fee"). Memorize one anchor per chapter, then connect them through the single margin rule.

Every result is a special case of "set marginal benefit equal to marginal cost"; market failures (monopoly, externalities, public goods, missing information) are exactly the cases where private margins differ from social margins.
